## What the question is asking

For each of our two study questions we were offered two alternative routes:
an established/default approach and a compositional or molecular
alternative. This document states which route we kept as the primary
analysis, which we kept as a robustness check, and why. In both cases we
did **not** pick just one: we kept the primary route *and* the alternative
route, because when both agree the conclusion is much stronger.

The guiding principle is simple: if a result only appears with one
measurement choice and disappears with another, you should not trust it. If
it survives both, you can say the result does not depend on that particular
choice.

## Question 1 — Community composition: Bray–Curtis vs. Aitchison distance

### The two routes

1. **Bray–Curtis distance on compositional shares.** This is the default in
   microbial ecology. It compares samples by how much their species
   proportions differ, giving more weight to abundant species. It is what
   Tuesday's ordination module used.
2. **Aitchison distance.** This transforms counts with centred log-ratios
   (CLR) and then uses Euclidean distance. It is the distance that respects
   the compositional nature of sequencing data: only the *ratios* between
   taxa carry information, not the absolute counts.

### Which we kept

We kept **Bray–Curtis as the primary analysis** and reported **Aitchison as
a robustness check**. We did not discard either.

### Reason

Bray–Curtis is the standard for microbiome ordination and PERMANOVA, so it
is the natural language in which to report the result. Aitchison is the
compositional-data alternative that answers the same question in a
mathematically correct way for relative-abundance data. If the two distances
gave opposite answers we would have to dig deeper; since they agree (R² ≈
0.03, p ≈ 0.15 for both), we can say the "no difference" conclusion does
not depend on the distance metric.

### What we read

- Anderson, M. J. (2001). A new method for non-parametric multivariate
  analysis of variance. *Austral Ecology*, 26(1), 32–46.
  https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00470.x — this is the
  PERMANOVA paper; it explains why the method uses a distance matrix and
  how R² and permutation p-values work.
- Aitchison, J. (1986). *The Statistical Analysis of Compositional Data*.
  Chapman & Hall — the foundation for Aitchison distance and the CLR
  transform. The key point is that compositional data live in a simplex,
  so Euclidean distances on raw proportions are misleading and distances
  should be computed on log-ratios.

## Question 2 — BV prevalence: clinical Nugent label vs. molecular community type

### The two routes

1. **Clinical BV label from the Nugent score.** Nugent scoring is the
   standard Gram-stain method: scores 0–3 are negative, 4–6 intermediate,
   7–10 positive for bacterial vaginosis. This is what a clinician would
   record.
2. **Molecular community type from the sequencing data.** Tuesday's anatomy
   module defined a community as *Lactobacillus*-dominated if more than 50%
   of reads belonged to *Lactobacillus* species, otherwise as anaerobe-type.
   This is a sequencing-based proxy for BV.

### Which we kept

We kept the **clinical Nugent label as the primary outcome** and reported
**the molecular community type as a secondary view**. Again, we kept both.

### Reason

The Nugent score is the clinical reference, so it is the right primary
outcome for asking whether BV is more common in one arm. The molecular
community type is an independent check: it is measured from the same
sequencing table, but it is not the clinical definition. If the two
measures disagreed, we would worry that the sequencing failed to capture
BV; since they agree (clinical label p = 0.45, molecular type p = 0.53, and
37 of 39 clinical positives are anaerobe-type), we can say the "no
difference" conclusion is not an artefact of how BV was defined.

### What we read

- Nugent, R. P., Krohn, M. A., & Hillier, S. L. (1991). Reliability of
  diagnosing bacterial vaginosis is improved by a standardized method of
  Gram stain interpretation. *Journal of Clinical Microbiology*, 29(2),
  297–301. https://doi.org/10.1128/jcm.29.2.297-301.1991 — this defines the
  Nugent score and explains why it became the standard.
- Ravel, J., Gajer, P., Abdo, Z., Schneider, G. M., Koenig, S. S. K.,
  McCulle, S. L., … Forney, L. J. (2011). Vaginal microbiome of
  reproductive-age women. *Proceedings of the National Academy of
  Sciences*, 108(supplement 1), 4680–4687.
  https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1002611107 — this paper describes vaginal
  community state types, including the lactobacillus-dominated types and
  the anaerobe types that correspond to BV.

## Bottom line

For **composition**, the primary result is the Bray–Curtis PERMANOVA, and
the Aitchison distance confirms it. For **BV**, the primary result is the
clinical Nugent label, and the molecular community type confirms it. In
both cases we kept both routes because agreement between them makes the
"no evidence of a difference" conclusion much more credible than either
route alone.
